children.text: Created by Kylie Warkentin.

This lesson is intended for use in sophomore level high school classrooms, though it could certainly be adapted for other grade levels in 9-12 education. It serves as an introduction to working with sound in poetry, comprising of two parts. Part I models how to close read and annotate a poem (paying particular attention to sound) using Langston Hughes’s “Harlem." In Part II, students will apply what they learned about close reading, annotation, sound, and other poetic devices to a poem from around the world of their choice, culminating in an informal oral analysis.
By the end of the ~60 minute lesson,
students will be able to:
closely read and annotate a poem, identifying and analyzing how sound and poetic devices contribute to its meaning;
apply this close-reading process independently to a poem of their choice; and
use textual evidence and analysis of sound and other poetic devices to explain how a poem explores a larger thematic question.
Students can work individually or in pairs. It is entirely self-paced for the students.
To deliver this lesson, simply provide this project link to students:
https://kywark.github.io/chorusofvoiceslesson/
For materials, students will need:
Laptop and headphones
Print out of
"Harlem" by Langston Hughes
Print out of their chosen poem (found in
"Part II: Explore Your Own Poem!"

Depending on your level of comfort with AVAnnotate, you can either require students to create their own AVAnnotate project with their annotations of their chosen poem and their recorded oral analyses, or you can simply provide students with a physical copy of their chosen poem and allow them to record their analyses in a method of your choosing (voice memo on phone, recording on laptop, handwritten analysis, etc.). For support on how students can build their own AVAnnotate project, please consult the instructions and resources
found in our documentation.
Students  will navigate through the lesson by reading, watching, and listening to the resources in the project. Anything that is
bolded
is an action item for students to read/watch/do; anything that's
bolded and underlined
is a question (or questions) that students will respond to in a method of your choosing (e.g., Google Doc, notebook paper, etc.). For ease of grading, the required written responses are listed below:
Part I: Harlem
2-3 observations about the jazz clip that plays in "Student Instructions."
Annotations for their first read/listen of "Harlem" from "Part I: Harlem (1/4)."
3-4 observations about how their annotations compare to the example from "Part I: Learn Harlem (2/4)."
Additional annotations addressing sound, idea, and form in "Harlem" from "Part I: Learn Harlem (2/4)."
Additional insights from how their annotations compare to the example from "Part I: Learn Harlem (3/4)."
Labeled poetic devices on their annotations of "Harlem" from "Part I: Learn Harlem (3/4)."
Additional poetic devices added to their "Harlem" annotations from the example in "Part I: Learn Harlem (4/4)."
Elaboration in their "Harlem" annotations of how the poetic devices in one moment convey Hughes's meaning in "Part I: Learn Harlem (4/4)."
2-3 sentence answer addressing what they believe Hughes is trying to convey at the bottom of their "Harlem" annotations.
Part II: Explore Your Own Poem!
N.B.: This portion of the lesson could be assigned for homework or in a following class.
Annotations (either as an AVAnnotate Project or on a print out of their chosen poem)
Analysis (either as a 3-5 minute oral analysis or handwritten analytical paragraph)
